passage: In their Chennai flat, five-year-old Naveen trails Kishore from room to room. "Appa, where are you going?" "Just to the balcony, kanna." Two minutes later: "Appa, you still love me?" "Always." At bedtime Naveen says he won't go to his cousin's sleepover next week. "What if you forget me?" Kishore sits on the bed. "Here's our plan. I drop you, we do two squeezes, I say 'see you at eight in the morning,' and at eight I'm there." Naveen squeezes back twice, practising.

qa.q: Where does Kishore say he is going?
qa.a: He says he is just going to the balcony.

qa.q: What is Naveen afraid of about the sleepover?
qa.a: He is afraid his father will forget him while he is away.

qa.q: What plan did Kishore offer, and why might it help?
qa.a: He offered a set goodbye with two squeezes and a clear pickup time, which makes the separation predictable instead of scary.

qa.q: What would change if Kishore had said, "Don't be silly, you're a big boy"?
qa.a: Naveen's fear would likely stay or grow, because he would feel brushed off instead of helped.

grounding: A five-year-old keeps checking where his father is and asking if he is loved, and his father answers the sleepover fear with a predictable goodbye plan.

passage:
"Amma, are you in the bathroom?"
"Yes, Lavanya. Still here."
"Are you still there?"
"Still here." Rajni opens the door. "That's five times since breakfast, chellam."
"Do you love me more than your office?"
"More than every office in the world."
"Then why are you going away two nights?"
Rajni kneels. "It's for work. Let's make a goodbye plan. I'll call at bedtime both nights and sing our moon song. You keep my blue scarf. And I'm back on Friday before your bath."
"Promise?"
"Friday, before your bath."
Lavanya wraps the scarf round her neck and checks it twice.

qa.q: What will Lavanya keep while Rajni is away?
qa.a: She will keep her mother's blue scarf.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's question about the office suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she is afraid of mattering less and worried about being left behind.

qa.q: Which choice helps Lavanya most, and why?
qa.a: Rajni gives a clear goodbye plan with bedtime calls, the scarf and a return time, so the separation feels predictable.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel hearing "Are you still there?" so often?
qa.a: She may feel a little worn by the questions but also tender, since she answers patiently each time.

grounding: A young girl keeps checking on her mother and asking if she is loved, and her mother responds to an upcoming trip with a predictable goodbye plan.

passage: Teacher's note, KG-B. Samir asked me six times this morning, "Is Mumma still at the gate?" At snack he whispered, "Does she love me even when I spill?" He will not come to Friday's class sleepover, and I will not push him. Today his mother, Vasudha, tried something new: the same hug and the same words at the gate, "I'll be here after the bell." Samir cried less. Next, I will give him a small job at drop-off, and we agreed to keep that goodbye exactly the same each day.

qa.q: How many times did Samir ask about Mumma this morning?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: What might Samir be worried about when he asks about spilling?
qa.a: He seems anxious that Mumma's love could change if he makes a mistake, so he needs reassurance.

qa.q: What small step did the adults agree on to help Samir?
qa.a: A goodbye that stays exactly the same each day, plus a small job for him at drop-off.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel when Samir cries less at the gate?
qa.a: She is probably relieved and hopeful that the steady goodbye is helping him.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps checking where a parent is and avoids a sleepover, helped by a predictable goodbye.

passage: In the fishing village near Karwar, Maria stayed so close to her mother Uma's sari that she nearly tripped her while she cleaned fish. "You won't go to the market without me?" "No." Ten minutes later: "You love me, na?" "Still yes." That night Maria was meant to sleep at her cousin's house two lanes away. An hour later her uncle walked her back, sobbing. Uma didn't scold. She sat on the step with her. "Tomorrow we'll try again. I'll walk you over and tell you when I'll come to fetch you."

qa.q: Who walked Maria back that night?
qa.a: Her uncle walked her back, sobbing.

qa.q: What does Maria's repeated "You love me, na?" suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: She seems anxious and unsure, needing to hear again and again that she is loved and that Uma won't leave.

qa.q: How could Uma help Maria manage the next night away?
qa.a: Keep doing what she started: stay calm, sit with her, walk her over and say exactly when she will fetch her.

qa.q: What would change if Uma had called Maria a baby for coming home?
qa.a: Maria would likely feel ashamed and even more afraid of being apart, making the next try harder.

grounding: Illustrates a child seeking constant reassurance and struggling to sleep away, helped by a calm, predictable plan.

passage: "Papá? Are you still there?" Siddiq called from bed for the fourth time, his voice small in the Madrid flat. Diego stopped washing up and went in. "Still here. Still love you." "Even though I kicked the ball at Lucía?" "Even then." Earlier at the park, Siddiq had run back to Diego's bench every few minutes just to touch his knee. Diego didn't tell him to stop being a baby, the way his own father once had. Instead he said, "I'll check on you when the dishes are done, and again when I brush my teeth." He did both times. The calls from bed got fewer.

qa.q: What did Siddiq do at the park?
qa.a: He ran back to Diego's bench every few minutes just to touch his knee.

qa.q: What might Siddiq be worried about when he asks about kicking the ball at Lucía?
qa.a: He seems afraid that doing something wrong could make his father stop loving him.

qa.q: Which choice of Diego's worked, and why?
qa.a: Promising two exact check-ins and keeping both, because it gave Siddiq something predictable to rely on.

qa.q: Why might Diego react differently from his own father?
qa.a: He may remember how it felt to be called a baby and want Siddiq to feel reassured instead of dismissed.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps checking on a parent and asking if he is loved, helped by predictable check-ins rather than dismissal.

passage:
At Sunshine Nursery, Rekha kept running to the window to check if Papa's scooter was still at the gate.
"Chandrika Miss, does Papa love me?"
"Yes."
Two minutes later: "Does he love me even if I cry?"
On Friday the class had a sleepover in the hall, and Rekha sobbed so hard her papa came to take her home.
The next week, Chandrika Miss helped Papa make a goodbye plan: two hugs, one wave from the gate, "Back at four."
By Thursday, Rekha stood at the window, waved once and went to the sand tray.

qa.q: What did Rekha keep checking from the window?
qa.a: Whether Papa's scooter was still at the gate.

qa.q: What was Rekha afraid of?
qa.a: She feared being separated from Papa and not being loved, so she kept asking if he loved her, even if she cried.

qa.q: Why did the goodbye plan help Rekha?
qa.a: The same two hugs, one wave and "Back at four" each day made the goodbye predictable, which calmed her fear better than being told not to worry.

qa.q: How might Chandrika Miss see Rekha's many questions?
qa.a: Chandrika Miss treats them as real fear, not naughtiness, and helps Papa build a steady routine instead of dismissing them.

grounding: Shows a child who checks on her father and asks if she is loved, and how a predictable goodbye helps her separation fear.
